lessons.title: KV caching & prefill/decode for multimodal computer-use agents
lessons.summary: Why agent loops are dominated by prefill vs decode: attention FLOPs O(n²) vs O(n), KV cache memory growth, multimodal screenshot token blowup, and harness choices (truncate, summarize, cache reuse, prefix sharing).

cards.q: You append one 2k-token screenshot to an 8k-token prefix that is already cached, then decode 50 tokens. Which term usually dominates wall-clock on a memory-bandwidth-bound decode stack, and why?
choices: Prefill of the new 2k tokens: attention work is O((10k)²) so the append alone dwarfs 50 decode steps
Prefill of only the new 2k tokens against the cached 8k (plus writing their KV), then 50 cheap O(n) decode steps — the incremental prefill is the spike; decode is rarely the larger bill here
The 50 decode steps: each must recompute Q,K,V for the whole 10k context
Neither: weight loading is identical for prefill and decode so they cost the same
cards.a: Prefill of only the new 2k tokens against the cached 8k (plus writing their KV), then 50 cheap O(n) decode steps — the incremental prefill is the spike; decode is rarely the larger bill here
cards.explanation: With a working prefix cache you do not re-prefill 8k. Incremental prefill still pays attention for the new tokens against the full prefix (and builds their KV). Each decode step is O(n·d) against the cache. For short tool replies (≈50 tokens) the append prefill usually dominates; long generated plans flip that.

cards.q: Why does switching from MHA to MQA shrink KV-cache memory far more than it shrinks prefill FLOPs?
choices: MQA deletes the feed-forward layers during prefill
KV memory scales with H_kv, so one shared K/V head cuts cache size by ~H; prefill FLOPs are dominated by dense matmuls over d_model, which barely change
MQA makes attention O(n) instead of O(n²) during prefill
MQA quantizes K and V to int8 automatically
cards.a: KV memory scales with H_kv, so one shared K/V head cuts cache size by ~H; prefill FLOPs are dominated by dense matmuls over d_model, which barely change
cards.explanation: Cache bytes ≈ 2·L·H_kv·d_head·n·bytes. MQA sets H_kv=1. Prefill is still ~2N FLOPs per token for an N-parameter model; attention is a smaller share for large models. Decode bandwidth to load the cache is where MQA/GQA win hardest.

cards.q: An agent re-sends the full multimodal trajectory every step with no prefix cache. Horizon is H observe→act cycles and each new screenshot adds ~S tokens. How does total prefill attention cost scale with H (rough order)?
choices: O(H) — each step only processes the newest screenshot
O(H² · S²) — step t re-prefills a context of length ~t·S, so Σ_t (tS)² ~ H³ S² wait — actually Σ_t (tS)² = S² Σ t² ~ S² H³
Σ_{t=1..H} O((t·S)²) ≈ O(S² H³) — naive full re-encode pays quadratic attention on a linearly growing context, every step
O(S²) independent of H because the model batches all screenshots
cards.a: Σ_{t=1..H} O((t·S)²) ≈ O(S² H³) — naive full re-encode pays quadratic attention on a linearly growing context, every step
cards.explanation: Context length n_t ≈ t·S. Prefill attention ~ n_t² per step. Summing t=1..H gives ~S²·H³/3. Prefix caching collapses that toward paying each new segment once (plus decode).

cards.q: KV cache for one sequence is ≈ 2·L·H_kv·d_head·n·bytes_per_elem. You double context length n and switch from MHA (H_kv=H) to GQA with H_kv=H/8. Net cache size vs the original MHA short context?
choices: 16× larger
Same size (2× from n, ÷8 from H_kv → ¼)
¼ of the original (2× from n, ÷8 from H_kv)
½ of the original
cards.a: ¼ of the original (2× from n, ÷8 from H_kv)
cards.explanation: Linear in both n and H_kv. Doubling n multiplies by 2; cutting H_kv by 8 multiplies by 1/8; product is 1/4.

cards.q: A computer-use harness must keep grounding fidelity on the latest screen but is OOMing on KV for a 40-step OSWorld-style trajectory of high-res screenshots. Which policy best matches the systems+ML trade-off in this lesson?
choices: Drop the latest screenshot and keep all historical raw images — history matters more than the current pixels
Keep the latest screenshot at full fidelity, summarize or drop older screenshots (or their KV), and reuse prefix cache for the stable system prompt + tool schema
Disable the KV cache so memory stays flat
Replace every screenshot with a 1-token caption and never send pixels again
cards.a: Keep the latest screenshot at full fidelity, summarize or drop older screenshots (or their KV), and reuse prefix cache for the stable system prompt + tool schema
cards.explanation: Grounding needs current pixels (Oct 11). History management is a systems problem: older frames are usually better as text summaries/ledger than as thousands of image tokens each. Prefix cache amortizes the static prompt.

cards.q: During decode, why is attention against a cached K,V only O(n·d) per new token rather than O(n²·d)?
choices: Softmax is skipped in decode
Only one new query row is multiplied by the n cached keys (and then by V); you do not rebuild the full n×n score matrix
FlashAttention changes the asymptotic complexity from quadratic to linear
Decode uses a CNN instead of attention
cards.a: Only one new query row is multiplied by the n cached keys (and then by V); you do not rebuild the full n×n score matrix
cards.explanation: Prefill builds Q,K,V for all n tokens and scores an n×n (masked) matrix ~O(n²d). Decode appends one token: one q against n keys → n scores → weighted sum of n value vectors → O(nd) per layer (plus the FFN).

cards.q: PagedAttention (vLLM) primarily helps serving by…
choices: Approximating attention with a linear kernel so FLOPs drop from O(n²) to O(n)
Storing each sequence's KV in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks (like OS virtual memory), cutting fragmentation and enabling sharing of common prefixes across requests
Replacing GQA with MHA for higher quality
Running prefill and decode on the CPU
cards.a: Storing each sequence's KV in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks (like OS virtual memory), cutting fragmentation and enabling sharing of common prefixes across requests
cards.explanation: KV grows/shrinks dynamically; contiguous reservation wastes memory. Paging gives near-zero waste and prefix sharing — critical when many agent sessions share a system prompt.

cards.q: Latent world-action models (Oct 15) cut per-step generative renders. How does that interact with today's prefill/decode picture?
choices: It removes the need for a KV cache entirely
It reduces decode and image-token prefill from K speculative futures, but the agent still pays growing multimodal context costs unless the harness caches prefixes and manages screenshot history
It makes prefill O(n) and decode O(n²)
It only helps training loss, never inference latency
cards.a: It reduces decode and image-token prefill from K speculative futures, but the agent still pays growing multimodal context costs unless the harness caches prefixes and manages screenshot history
cards.explanation: Yesterday attacked K× render + K× re-perceive. Today's bottleneck is the base observe→act context: screenshots + tool traces still grow n. You need both algorithmic foresight and systems-level cache/history policy.

lessons.title: Latent world action models for GUI agents
lessons.summary: Why pixel-space GUI world models hit identity shortcuts and latency walls: Render-and-Re-Perceive, latent action+transition heads on shared LMM reps, action-aware contrastive objectives, and what this means for computer-use harnesses.

cards.q: Why does the identity shortcut (predicting a future screen ≈ the current one) get worse as GUI transitions get larger?
choices: Large transitions contain more pixels than the decoder can output
A pointwise loss is minimized by the conditional mean; large transitions have many weakly-constrained outcomes whose differences cancel, so the shared component (the current screen) dominates
Large transitions are always rarer in the training set
Optical flow fails on text, so the model ignores text regions
cards.a: A pointwise loss is minimized by the conditional mean; large transitions have many weakly-constrained outcomes whose differences cancel, so the shared component (the current screen) dominates
cards.explanation: GUI transitions are discontinuous (an auth wall or new page), unlike flow-continuous video. More plausible futures means a blurrier conditional mean that regresses toward the present. Copying s_t is the cheapest way to lower the loss.

cards.q: Per decision step with K candidates, what does Render-and-Re-Perceive need at inference that the latent world-action model does not?
choices: A base agent to propose candidates
K generative renders of future screens plus K scorer passes that re-perceive them
An encoding of the current screenshot
A goal description
cards.a: K generative renders of future screens plus K scorer passes that re-perceive them
cards.explanation: The latent method drops the transition head at inference and reads K index-token logits from one forward pass over a prompt that contains all K candidates.

cards.q: Why isn't using only the current state z_t as the contrastive negative enough, e.g., for 'Sort: Most popular' vs 'Sort: Closest'?
choices: Because z_t equals z_{t+1} for sort actions

Both predictions can move away from z_t in the same generic 'something changed' direction; negatives from other transitions (the memory bank) force the prediction to match this action's specific future
InfoNCE needs at least two positives
Temperature cancels with a single negative
cards.a: Both predictions can move away from z_t in the same generic 'something changed' direction; negatives from other transitions (the memory bank) force the prediction to match this action's specific future
cards.explanation: The z_t negative is anti-copy, and the bank negatives are anti-generic. You need both to get action-specific consequence features.

cards.q: Why put all K candidates in one prompt in random order and predict the annotated action's next state from the single shared final-token state h_t?
choices: To reduce image tokens
So h_t must encode which candidate is correct and what it leads to, instead of relying on a position prior, which couples future-state supervision to the features the action head scores with
Because LoRA cannot touch per-candidate tokens
So the transition head can be used at inference
cards.a: So h_t must encode which candidate is correct and what it leads to, instead of relying on a position prior, which couples future-state supervision to the features the action head scores with
cards.explanation: Both losses update the same LoRA backbone. The world-model objective works as a representation regularizer on the reranker.

cards.q: If the correct action is absent from the base agent's K candidates, what can the latent world-action model do?
choices: Generate the missing action from the predicted latent
Nothing: it only re-ranks proposals, so success is bounded by candidate coverage
Retrieve it from the contrastive memory bank
Fall back to a pixel world model
cards.a: Nothing: it only re-ranks proposals, so success is bounded by candidate coverage
cards.explanation: Fixes are upstream: more diverse sampling, adaptive K, better proposers. During training, steps with no matching candidate are labeled with the agent's own top-1.

cards.q: What is the main trade-off of discarding the transition head at inference?
choices: The action head stops working
Foresight adds no inference cost, but it lives only implicitly in h_t: no inspectable predicted future and no multi-step latent rollout
Accuracy drops to the base agent's level
The model must regenerate pixels
cards.a: Foresight adds no inference cost, but it lives only implicitly in h_t: no inspectable predicted future and no multi-step latent rollout
cards.explanation: Prediction is a training-time shaping signal. The paper lists one-step-only prediction and lack of interpretability as limitations.

cards.q: A confidence gate invokes the judge only when the agent is unsure. Which errors can it never catch, and what's a sensible harness fix?
choices: Low-confidence errors; lower the threshold
High-confidence agent errors bypass rescoring; force rescoring for irreversible actions or learn an uncertainty-aware invocation policy
Duplicate-candidate errors; raise τ
Grounding errors; re-enable the transition head
cards.a: High-confidence agent errors bypass rescoring; force rescoring for irreversible actions or learn an uncertainty-aware invocation policy
cards.explanation: Gating trades coverage for compute and depends on calibrated proposer confidence. Send, pay, and delete steps are worth one judge pass regardless of confidence.

cards.q: Offline, latent rescoring improves action-type accuracy more consistently than click grounding accuracy. Why?
choices: The contrastive loss degrades spatial features
Rescoring changes which candidate is chosen but never refines a candidate's coordinates, so grounding stays the proposer's job
Grounding is evaluated on a different dataset
The action head outputs coordinates at low resolution
cards.a: Rescoring changes which candidate is chosen but never refines a candidate's coordinates, so grounding stays the proposer's job
cards.explanation: A reranker can fix 'scroll vs tap search' type errors. It cannot move a slightly-off click into the right bounding box.

lessons.title: Temporal credit assignment: from REINFORCE to process rewards
lessons.summary: Why sparse terminal rewards make long computer-use trajectories nearly unlearnable: REINFORCE variance, baselines and advantage, GAE intuition, and how process/step rewards (and OSWorld-style checkpoints) reshape credit assignment.

cards.q: With a single terminal reward and γ=1, how does G_t compare for early vs late actions on the same trajectory?
choices: Early actions get larger G_t because more future rewards remain
G_t equals the same terminal reward for every timestep
Only the last action gets nonzero G_t
G_t is always 1/T
cards.a: G_t equals the same terminal reward for every timestep
cards.explanation: Sparse terminal reward smears identical credit/blame across every action in the episode — the core temporal credit assignment failure for long GUI rollouts.

cards.q: Why does subtracting a state-only baseline b(s) not bias the REINFORCE gradient?
choices: Because b cancels in the TD error by definition
Because E[∇ log π(a|s) · b(s)] = 0 for any function of s alone
Because baselines are trained with a separate orthogonalizing loss
Because autograd stops gradients through b
cards.a: Because E[∇ log π(a|s) · b(s)] = 0 for any function of s alone
cards.explanation: Σ_a π ∇ log π = ∇ Σ_a π = ∇1 = 0. Baselines cut variance without changing the expected gradient.

cards.q: You add checkpoint rewards (+1 when each subgoal holds) instead of only terminal pass/fail. What should happen to credit assignment?
choices: Policy-gradient variance must increase because more terms are random
Effective credit horizon shrinks: actions that hit a checkpoint get signal before episode end
The gradient is unbiased only if GAE uses λ=1
Grounding accuracy drops because the action space is unchanged
cards.a: Effective credit horizon shrinks: actions that hit a checkpoint get signal before episode end
cards.explanation: Process/step rewards make G_t differ across timesteps so intermediate progress is attributable — the same reason PRMs beat pure outcome rewards on multi-step tasks.

cards.q: GAE λ→0 vs λ→1: which is correct?
choices: λ→0 is Monte Carlo; λ→1 is 1-step TD
λ→0 is 1-step TD (more bias, less variance); λ→1 recovers the Monte Carlo advantage G_t−V(s_t)
λ only retunes γ, not the estimator family
λ→0 and λ→1 are identical under sparse rewards
cards.a: λ→0 is 1-step TD (more bias, less variance); λ→1 recovers the Monte Carlo advantage G_t−V(s_t)
cards.explanation: Â_t = Σ_l (γλ)^l δ_{t+l}. Middle λ values are the bias–variance dial used in modern on-policy LLM-RL.

cards.q: A process reward gives +1 for 'export file exists' even when contents are wrong. What goes wrong?
choices: Baseline bias in REINFORCE
Reward hacking: a misspecified proxy reinforces trajectories that satisfy the proxy but not the true goal
GAE λ set too low
Screenshots are partially observable
cards.a: Reward hacking: a misspecified proxy reinforces trajectories that satisfy the proxy but not the true goal
cards.explanation: Dense rewards help only if they track the real objective. Cheap existence checks are exactly the false 'done' signal long-horizon agents already abuse.

cards.q: 5-step export: steps 1–3 correct, wrong folder at 4, confirm at 5; sparse terminal fail. What does REINFORCE get from this episode?
choices: Only step 4 receives a negative update
Zero gradient contribution from every action — the failure is silent
Steps 1–3 get positive updates for partial progress
Step 5 absorbs all the blame as the action nearest the reward
cards.a: Zero gradient contribution from every action — the failure is silent
cards.explanation: r_T=0 ⇒ G_t=0 for all t. Sparse failure does not localize blame; process rewards that zero out after the bad checkpoint would.

cards.q: You have a good value baseline but still only terminal reward on 300-step jobs. What remains hard?
choices: Baselines will bias the policy gradient, so avoid them
Advantages cut variance, but early and late actions can still share nearly the same G_t, so intermediate credit stays weak
GAE is undefined without process rewards
REINFORCE cannot use neural policies
cards.a: Advantages cut variance, but early and late actions can still share nearly the same G_t, so intermediate credit stays weak
cards.explanation: A_t = r_T − V(s_t) still hinges on one Bernoulli. Densify rewards or learn a strong long-horizon critic — baselines alone do not invent step-level credit.

lessons.title: OSWorld 2.0: Why computer-use agents still fail long-horizon work
lessons.summary: OSWorld 2.0 (June 2026) moved computer-use evals from ~2-minute tasks to 1.6-hour workflows: best paper result 20.6% binary / 54.8% partial. Ten challenge phenomena, horizon collapse, stale-state and streaming failures, safety findings, how to read Oct 2026 leaderboard numbers, and harness design takeaways.

cards.q: OSWorld 2.0 paper's best result (Claude Opus 4.8, max thinking, batched tool calls, 500 steps)?
choices: 83.5% binary
20.6% binary / 54.8% partial
44.33% binary / 77.67% partial
81.8% partial
cards.a: 20.6% binary / 54.8% partial
cards.explanation: 83.5% is Opus 4.8 on OSWorld-Verified (1.0); 44.33/77.67 is a later Snorkel-board Opus 5 row; 81.8% partial is Anthropic's Opus 5.5 on the osworld-v2.1 task release.

cards.q: Name the four task-level failure patterns the OSWorld 2.0 authors highlight.
cards.a: Agents lose track of constraints, miss information that arrives mid-task, guess rather than ask the user, and skip verification.
cards.explanation: Not basic GUI control or coding: local actions are fine, the task-level model drifts.

cards.q: How does OSWorld 2.0 scale vs 1.0 (human time, agent steps, scoring)?
cards.a: Median human time ~1.6 h vs ~2 min (~48x); >250 agent steps vs ~30; binary plus partial scoring over ~27.25 weighted final-state checkpoints per task.
cards.explanation: Also 31 self-hosted websites, a simulated user, injected mid-task messages, and a separate safety audit.

cards.q: Why does a streaming UI (moving pop-up) break a correctly grounded click?
choices: Coordinate scaling bug
The click is stale: right for the screenshot, wrong for the screen at action time
Missing accessibility tree
Wrong referring expression
cards.a: The click is stale: right for the screenshot, wrong for the screen at action time
cards.explanation: A timing failure of the discrete screenshot-think-act loop; shrink observe-to-act latency or re-observe right before acting.

cards.q: Which OSWorld 2.0 phenomena were weakest across agents?
cards.a: Hidden-state ones: implicit-state inference, multi-item state tracking, conflict disambiguation, and dynamic environment.
cards.explanation: They demand state the instruction does not give directly, and keeping it current as the task evolves.

cards.q: Roughly what share of budget did agents spend on recovery + repair, and why does it matter?
choices: Under 7%
About 25%
About 50%
Over 80%
cards.a: Under 7%
cards.explanation: Errors compound over hundreds of steps; explicit monitoring and self-repair is flagged by the authors as a clear lever.

cards.q: A vendor posts '80% on OSWorld 2.1'. What do you check before comparing it to the paper?
cards.a: Metric (binary vs partial), task release (osworld-v2.1 vs 2026.06.24/08.08), step budget, effort level, and who ran it (plus active safeguards/fallbacks).
cards.explanation: Anthropic's OSWorld 2.1 numbers are partial scores; compare to 54.8% partial, not 20.6% binary, and still with caveats. Snorkel's board shows a 13-point binary spread within one model/effort label.

cards.q: Task 035 (purchase orders): why did the agent's final self-check miss an approved request?
cards.a: It froze its working set at 'now I have all the information' and checked the sheet against its own incomplete internal list instead of re-reconciling all sources after late messages.
cards.explanation: Fix: externalized task ledger, treat new messages as invalidation events, verify against independent checkpoints.

lessons.title: How computer-use agents ground actions to screen coordinates
lessons.summary: How VLM agents turn instructions into screen clicks: element IDs vs coordinate tokens, normalized vs pixel coords, rescaling pitfalls, key models, ScreenSpot benchmarks, and practical tips.

cards.q: Model input is 1280x800, real screen 2560x1600; model outputs click(640,400). Where should the harness click?
cards.explanation: Scale each axis by real/model size (x2). (0.5,0.5) is the normalized point, not pixels.

cards.q: Why is plain token cross-entropy awkward for coordinate prediction?
cards.a: It treats numbers as categories, so near misses (499 vs 500) get no partial credit; distance-aware rewards or location bins help.
cards.explanation: Motivates RL with hit/distance rewards for grounding.

cards.q: Main advantage and main weakness of Set-of-Marks / accessibility-tree element IDs?
cards.a: Exact clicks via ID-to-box mapping, but depends on a detector or a11y tree that may be missing (canvas apps, remote desktops).

cards.q: Why do models score far lower on ScreenSpot-Pro than ScreenSpot?
choices: Non-English instructions only
High-res professional apps with tiny targets
Mobile-only screenshots
Missing ground truth
cards.a: High-res professional apps with tiny targets
cards.explanation: Best baseline at release was 18.9% (OS-Atlas-7B); ScreenSeekeR visual search reached 48.1% training-free.

cards.q: What coordinate format does Qwen2-VL/Qwen3-VL use for grounding?
cards.a: Relative coordinates on a 0-1000 grid; pixel = value/1000 x image size.
cards.explanation: Resolution-invariant, unlike absolute pixel outputs.

cards.q: You letterbox a 16:9 screenshot into a 4:3 input but rescale with simple width/height ratios. Symptom?
choices: Random clicks
Systematic offset along the padded axis
No effect
Only text targets fail
cards.a: Systematic offset along the padded axis
cards.explanation: Subtract padding before scaling.

cards.q: Training-free technique to improve grounding of tiny targets on huge screens?
cards.a: Coarse-to-fine cropping / visual search: predict a region, crop, re-ground at higher effective resolution.

cards.q: Cheapest large-scale source of GUI grounding training data?
cards.a: Rendered web pages with DOM element boxes and text/aria labels (used by SeeClick, UGround, OS-Atlas).
